issues.legal_issue: The environmental tribunal has jurisdiction to hear a representative application seeking environmental relief and compensation for harm caused by an activity governed by environmental law, even when the deceased persons’ legal representatives have not applied.
material_facts: A registered representative organization applied to the environmental tribunal for restoration of a hill damaged by mineral extraction and for protective directions after flooding on a highway caused two deaths.
The mineral lease covered more than five hectares, and the record did not show that the required environmental clearance had been obtained.
The deceased persons’ legal representatives had not applied to the tribunal and had instead commenced a civil suit.
issues.conclusion: The tribunal had jurisdiction to entertain the application and grant environmental relief and compensation; the absence of the deceased persons’ legal representatives did not bar it from doing so.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 14, 15(1)(a)–(c), 15(4), 17 and 18(2) of the National Green Tribunal Act, 2010, the tribunal has primary jurisdiction over substantial environmental questions, independent restorative powers, and authority to grant compensation for death, injury and environmental damage. Section 15(1)(b) and (c) are not confined to violations of enactments in Schedule I; Section 17 provides for compensation where death or damage results from an activity under a Schedule I enactment. Section 18(2) permits an aggrieved representative body to apply, and the proviso concerning legal representatives does not require rejection of an application when they have not joined. The court relied on Mantri Techzone Pvt. Ltd. v. Forward Foundation, State of Meghalaya v. All Dimasa Students Union, Hinch Lal Tiwari v. Kamala Devi, and Jitendra Singh v. Ministry of Environment.

rule.if: ngt_environmental_proceeding and environmental_harm_from_regulated_activity and activity_lacked_required_clearance and aggrieved_representative_applicant and deceased_heirs_not_applicants

predicates.ngt_environmental_proceeding: An applicant brought a dispute concerning environmental harm before the environmental tribunal.
predicates.environmental_harm_from_regulated_activi: An activity governed by environmental regulation caused environmental harm.
predicates.activity_lacked_required_clearance: The person undertaking the activity did not obtain a required environmental clearance.
predicates.aggrieved_representative_applicant: A representative organization claiming to be aggrieved applied to the tribunal for relief.
predicates.deceased_heirs_not_applicants: The legal representatives of people who died in the incident did not join the tribunal application.

issues.definition: When an aggrieved representative organization brings an environmental proceeding about harm from an activity lacking required clearance, the tribunal has jurisdiction to grant environmental relief and compensation even if deceased persons’ heirs did not apply.

issues.legal_issue: Compensation for deaths and environmental restoration is justified where a highway authority and a person responsible for nearby hill damage knew of a foreseeable drainage danger and failed to take remedial measures, subject to independent determination of final liability in a civil suit.
material_facts: The highway authority was responsible for maintaining the highway and had contracted for its operation and maintenance, including safety monitoring and remedial work.

Inspection reports and correspondence identified deficient drainage, debris, and a risk to highway safety before the incident; the highway authority and the mineral extractor were aware of the danger.
Hill cutting and accumulated debris contributed to blocked drainage channels, and flooding swept away a car on the highway, killing two occupants.
The tribunal ordered compensation for the deceased persons’ legal representatives and payment for environmental restoration.
The legal representatives had filed a civil suit, which the Supreme Court directed to proceed so that liability and apportionment could be determined independently on evidence.
issues.conclusion: The compensation and environmental-restoration directions against the highway authority and the mineral extractor were upheld as a prima facie determination. The civil suit must proceed, and its court must independently decide final liability and apportionment.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 15 and 17 of the National Green Tribunal Act authorize relief for death and restoration of the environment. Sections 4 and 5 of the National Highways Act, 1956, read with Section 16 of the National Highways Authority of India Act, 1988, place responsibility for highway maintenance on the relevant public authority. A public authority may incur liability where its conduct or omission breaches a duty of care and causes injury; a known danger and failure to take remedial measures may support liability. The court relied on Rajkot Municipal Corpn. v. Manjulben Jayantilal Nakum, Municipal Corpn. of Delhi v. Sushila Devi, Vadodara Municipal Corporation v. Purshottam V. Muranji, and M.C. Mehta v. Union of India. The tribunal’s compensation determination did not conclusively resolve liability in the pending civil suit.

rule.if: ngt_compensation_and_restoration_proceeding and highway_maintenance_duty and known_foreseeable_drainage_danger and responsible_actors_failed_to_remedy and fatal_flooding_and_environmental_damage_resulted

predicates.ngt_compensation_and_restoration_proceed: An environmental tribunal proceeding sought compensation for deaths and restoration of environmental damage.
predicates.highway_maintenance_duty: A highway authority was responsible for maintaining the highway and its drainage arrangements.
predicates.known_foreseeable_drainage_danger: Reports or communications informed the authority and another responsible actor of a drainage danger before the incident.
predicates.responsible_actors_failed_to_remedy: The authority and the other responsible actor failed to take remedial measures after the danger was identified.
predicates.fatal_flooding_and_environmental_damage_: Flooding associated with the drainage obstruction caused deaths and environmental damage.
predicates.civil_suit_pending: The deceased persons’ legal representatives had brought a civil suit concerning liability for the incident.

issues.definition: When an environmental compensation proceeding concerns fatal flooding and environmental damage following a known, unremedied drainage danger, prima facie compensation and restoration orders may stand while a pending civil suit independently determines final liability.

issues.legal_issue: The environmental tribunal may issue general directions for future environmental protection, but a blanket development restriction unsupported by scientific or expert material and proper consideration of the evidence is improper.
material_facts: The tribunal directed revenue and municipal authorities to impose a uniform restriction on construction near hills and hilltops.
The tribunal relied on limited incident-related material and did not obtain scientific or technical evidence or an expert opinion supporting the uniform restriction.
The tribunal did not follow the process of obtaining and considering expert reports and allowing parties to address that material, as had been done in other environmental cases.
issues.conclusion: The tribunal has power to issue general directions for future environmental guidance, but the particular blanket restriction was unsupported and procedurally indefensible and was set aside.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 15(1)(b) and (c) of the National Green Tribunal Act and Section 19, together with Rule 24 of the National Green Tribunal (Practice and Procedure) Rules, 2011, empower the tribunal to make remedial and preventive directions, including general directions for future guidance. That power must be exercised on a reasoned basis and, where the issue requires scientific or technical assessment, with appropriate expert input and consideration of the material by the parties. The court relied on State of Meghalaya v. All Dimasa Students Union, Mantri Techzone Pvt. Ltd. v. Forward Foundation, Hanuman Laxman Aroskar v. Union of India, and Tamil Nadu Pollution Control Board v. Sterlite Industries (I) Ltd.

predicates.ngt_case_with_general_environmental_dire: The environmental tribunal issued a direction in a case that was intended to guide conduct beyond the parties before it.
predicates.direction_imposes_blanket_development_re: The direction imposed a uniform restriction on development across a broad area or category of land.
predicates.no_scientific_or_expert_basis: The tribunal issued the restriction without scientific or technical evidence or an expert opinion supporting it.
predicates.expert_material_not_tested_by_parties: The tribunal did not obtain and consider expert material through a process that allowed the parties to address it.

issues.definition: A blanket development restriction issued by the environmental tribunal without scientific or expert support and without party consideration of expert material is set aside.

issues.legal_issue: A state planning authority may not impose a blanket planning restriction by administrative direction without adequate reasons and a proper basis, particularly where the direction effectively changes planning schemes without the prescribed planning process.
material_facts: The state issued a direction restricting development near hills and limiting additional development rights in areas already developed.
The state’s direction was based solely on the environmental tribunal’s unsupported restriction; the state produced no material or file showing independent reasons or expert input.
The direction did not define the landforms to which it applied and operated as a blanket change to regional and development plans without consultation or consideration of affected parties.
issues.conclusion: The state direction was arbitrary and was quashed; the High Court judgment upholding it was set aside.
issues.legal_principle: Section 154 of the Maharashtra Regional and Town Planning Act, 1966, as amended, permits state directions for specified public purposes and efficient administration, but that power must be exercised for good and adequate reasons and cannot be used to bypass the Act’s procedures for preparing or modifying planning schemes. The planning provisions require public notice, consideration of objections and suggestions, and opportunities to be heard for relevant plan changes. Administrative and delegated decisions must rest on relevant considerations and a rational basis. The court relied on T. Vijayalakshmi v. Town Planning Member, Pune Municipal Corpn. v. Promoters and Builders Assn., MIG Cricket Club v. Abhinav Sahakar Education Society, Shri Sitaram Sugar Mills Co. v. Union of India, and Cellular Operators Association v. Telecom Regulatory Authority of India.

rule.if: challenge_to_state_planning_direction and direction_makes_blanket_change_to_plans and direction_based_only_on_unsupported_external_order and no_independent_reasons_or_expert_basis and prescribed_public_planning_process_not_followed

predicates.challenge_to_state_planning_direction: A party challenged a state direction affecting land development and planning.
predicates.direction_makes_blanket_change_to_plans: The direction imposes a broad restriction that effectively changes existing regional or development plans.
predicates.direction_based_only_on_unsupported_exte: The state adopted the direction solely because another body had issued an unsupported direction.
predicates.no_independent_reasons_or_expert_basis: The state provided no independent reasons or expert material supporting its restriction.
predicates.prescribed_public_planning_process_not_f: The state imposed the restriction without following the applicable process for public notice, objections, and consideration of affected parties.

issues.definition: A state planning direction that makes a blanket plan change solely on an unsupported external order, without independent reasons or the prescribed public planning process, is arbitrary and quashed.

issues.legal_issue: A later proposed planning amendment does not prejudice development plans or development approvals that were already approved before the amendment was issued.
material_facts: The challenged state direction was issued after some plans and developments had already been approved.
The court considered whether those prior approvals could be disturbed by the later direction.
issues.conclusion: Plans and developments approved before the challenged direction could not be disturbed or adversely affected by it.
issues.legal_principle: Town-planning legislation is regulatory, and rights under existing approvals cannot be prejudiced merely because a later planning change is proposed or remains uncertain; changes must be made through the process authorized by law. The court relied on T. Vijayalakshmi v. Town Planning Member.

predicates.planning_case: The dispute concerns a planning direction or proposed change to land-use controls.
predicates.development_plan_or_project_approved_bef: A development plan or project received approval before the later planning change was issued.
predicates.later_change_would_prejudice_that_approv: The later planning change would adversely affect the previously approved plan or project.

issues.definition: When a planning change would adversely affect a development plan or project approved earlier, that earlier approval is not prejudiced by the later change.
